l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is a Argive
q: For there was a certain Myscelos, the son of Alemon, an Argive, most favoured by the Gods in those times.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hercules possesses Hercules's oxen (oxen of Iberia)
q: The son of Jove, enriched with the oxen of Iberia, is said to have reached the Lacinian shores,[1] from the ocean, after a prosperous voyage

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hercules is a son of Amphitryon (putative son)
q: He gives thanks to the parent, the son of Amphitryon,[3]

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hercules aids the sentence (to a favourable one)
q: Soon as it, being inverted, poured forth the pebbles to be counted, the colour of them all was changed from black to white, and the sentence, changed to a favourable one by the aid of Hercules, acquitted the son of Alemon.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hercules performs Twelve Labours
q: Oh thou! for whom the twice six labours have created the privilege of the heavens, aid me, I pray; for thou wast the cause of my offence.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius is destined for sovereign power (by Fame)
q: Fame, the harbinger of truth, destines the illustrious Numa for the sovereign power.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius knows Sabine nation (its ceremonials)
q: He does not deem it sufficient to be acquainted with the ceremonials of the Sabine nation

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius inquires into nature of things (as part of his expansive intellectual pursuits)
q: in his expansive mind he conceives greater views, and inquires into the nature of things.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Alemon is parent of Myscelos (father)
q: For there was a certain Myscelos, the son of Alemon, an Argive, most favoured by the Gods in those times.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Amphitryon is parent of Hercules (putative father)
q: Hercules was the putative son of Amphitryon, king of Thebes, who was the husband of his mother Alcmena.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Alcmena is parent of Hercules (mother)
q: Hercules was the putative son of Amphitryon, king of Thebes, who was the husband of his mother Alcmena.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is a son of Alemon
q: For there was a certain Myscelos, the son of Alemon, an Argive, most favoured by the Gods in those times.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsar is a river (in Calabria)
q: he finds the destined mouth of the river Æsar

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ionian Sea is crossed by Myscelos (during his voyage to Italy)
q: He gives thanks to the parent, the son of Amphitryon,[3] and with favouring gales sails over the Ionian sea

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is favoured by Gods (in those times)
q: For there was a certain Myscelos, the son of Alemon, an Argive, most favoured by the Gods in those times.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: oracle directs Myscelos (to settle where he encounters rain in a clear sky)
q: Myscelus, having consulted the oracle, concerning the colony which he was about to lead into a foreign country, was told that he must settle at the place where he should meet with rain in a clear sky

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos receives commands in Myscelos's dream (from Hercules)
q: Lying upon him, as he is overwhelmed with the drowsiness of sleep, the club-bearer, {Hercules}, addresses him: ‘Come, {now}, desert thy native abodes; go, {and} repair to the pebbly streams of the distant Æsar.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is subject to law forbidding Argives to leave Argos (when attempting to depart from Argos)
q: The Deity orders him to depart; the laws forbid his going; and death has been awarded as the punishment of him who attempts to leave his country.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is acquitted in Myscelos's trial (through the aid of Hercules)
q: Soon as it, being inverted, poured forth the pebbles to be counted, the colour of them all was changed from black to white, and the sentence, changed to a favourable one by the aid of Hercules, acquitted the son of Alemon.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos settles in Italy (after leaving Argos)
q: He retires to Italy, where he builds the city of Crotona.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos founds his walls (on the appointed land)
q: And there, on the appointed land, did he found his walls, and he transferred the name of him that was {there} entombed to his city.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hercules is a son of Jove
q: The son of Jove, enriched with the oxen of Iberia, is said to have reached the Lacinian shores,[1] from the ocean, after a prosperous voyage

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is a Samian by birth
q: There was a man, a Samian by birth; but he had fled from both Samos and its rulers,[8] and, through hatred of tyranny, he was a voluntary exile.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: animal sacrifice is attributed to Gods (wrongly, according to Pythagoras)
q: And it is not enough for such wickedness to be committed; they have imputed to the Gods themselves this abomination; and they believe that a Deity in the heavens can rejoice in the slaughter of the laborious ox.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the transmigration of souls is a continuing passage of souls between bodies (including animals and humans)
q: The soul wanders about and comes from that spot to this, from this to that, and takes possession of any limbs whatever; it both passes from the beasts to human bodies, and {so does} our {soul} into the beasts; and in no {lapse} of time does it perish.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the soul is immortal not subject to death (according to Pythagoras)
q: Souls are not subject to death; and having left their former abode, they ever inhabit new dwellings, and, {there} received, live on.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Euphorbus is a former identity of the soul (Pythagoras claims to remember being him)
q: I, myself, for I remember it, in the days of the Trojan war, was Euphorbus,[11] the son of Panthoüs

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Juno has temple at Argos (in the realm of Abas)
q: I lately recognised the shield, {once} the burden of my left arm, in the temple of Juno, at Argos, the realm of Abas.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Time is a constant progression (likened to a flowing river)
q: Even time itself glides on with a constant progress, no otherwise than a river.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: change and transformation is universal all things (nothing remains in the same form)
q: All things are flowing {onward},[12] and every shape is assumed in a fleeting course.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is exiled from Samos (voluntarily, through hatred of tyranny)
q: There was a man, a Samian by birth; but he had fled from both Samos and its rulers,[8] and, through hatred of tyranny, he was a voluntary exile.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the four elements are contained in the universe (as everlasting elementary bodies)
q: The everlasting universe contains four elementary bodies.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the four elements consist of earth, water, air, and fire (two heavy and two light elements)
q: Two of these, {namely}, earth and water, are heavy, and are borne downwards by their weight; and as many are devoid of weight, and air, and fire still purer than air, nothing pressing them, seek the higher regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the globe is a heavy element (borne downward by its weight)
q: Two of these, {namely}, earth and water, are heavy, and are borne downwards by their weight

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: water is a heavy element (borne downward by its weight)
q: Two of these, {namely}, earth and water, are heavy, and are borne downwards by their weight

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: air is a light element (seeking the higher regions)
q: and as many are devoid of weight, and air, and fire still purer than air, nothing pressing them, seek the higher regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras teaches Pythagorean philosophy (publicly, after studying the nature of things)
q: And when he had examined all things with his mind, and with watchful study, he gave them to be learned by the public

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: fire is a light element (purer than air and seeking the higher regions)
q: and as many are devoid of weight, and air, and fire still purer than air, nothing pressing them, seek the higher regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the elements' cycle of transformation transforms the four elements (in a recurring cycle)
q: Both the earth dissolving distils into flowing water; the water, too, evaporating, departs in the breezes and the air; its weight being removed again, the most subtle air shoots upwards into the fires {of the æther} on high. Thence do they return back again, and the same order is unravelled; for fire becoming gross, passes into dense air; this {changes} into water, and earth is formed of the water made dense.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the universe contains the four elements (everlasting)
q: The everlasting universe contains four elementary bodies.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the universe preserves all things (despite changes of form)
q: And, believe me, in this universe so vast, nothing perishes; but it varies and changes its appearance

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: animals include the horse, and the sheep, and the herds (animals that subsist on grass)
q: for the horse, and the sheep, and the herds subsist on grass.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: animals are subject to the transmigration of souls (souls pass between beasts and human bodies)
q: it both passes from the beasts to human bodies, and {so does} our {soul} into the beasts

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the sea changes into land (in places formerly covered by water)
q: I have seen land made from the sea; and far away from the ocean the sea-shells lay, and old anchors were found {there} on the tops of the mountains.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras investigates the origin and nature of the universe (through mental inquiry)
q: and wondered at the revealed origin of the vast universe, and the cause of things, and what nature {meant}, and what was God

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Leucas is surrounded by the sea (formerly annexed to the continent)
q: The ancient inhabitants had Leucas[22] annexed to the continent; now the sea surrounds it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Zancle was once united to Italy (later separated by the sea)
q: Zancle,[23] too, is said to have been united to Italy, until the sea cut off the neighbouring region

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is heard by Numa Pompilius (drawn by his reputation)
q: His reputation draws Numa Pompilius to hear his discourses

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras forbids animal sacrifice (as food served at table)
q: He, too, was the first to forbid animals to be served up at table

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras advocates vegetarianism (because animal flesh pollutes human bodies)
q: Forbear, mortals, to pollute your bodies with {such} abominable food. There is the corn; there are the apples that bear down the branches by their weight, and {there are} the grapes swelling upon the vines; there are the herbs that are pleasant

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: vegetarianism is available from the earth (without slaughter and bloodshed)
q: The lavish Earth yields her riches, and her agreable food, and affords dainties without slaughter and bloodshed.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is a philosopher
q: As Pythagoras was considered to have pursued metaphysical studies more deeply, perhaps, than any other of the ancient philosophers, Ovid could not have introduced a personage more fitted to discuss these subjects.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: change and transformation is a continual change (in the physical world)
q: The principle of Pythagoras, that everything is continually changing and that nothing perishes, is true to a certain extent; but in his times, and even in those of Ovid, philosophy was not sufficiently advanced to speak with precision on the subject, and to discover the true boundary between truth and fiction.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: human souls enter animals (as their abode through transmigration)
q: We too, {who are} a portion of the universe, (since we are not only bodies, but are fleeting souls as well, and can enter into beasts {as our} abode, and be hidden within the breasts of the cattle)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: vegetarian abstinence is practiced by Pythagorean philosophy (because souls may inhabit animals)
q: In consequence of this doctrine, it was a favourite tenet of his followers to abstain from eating the flesh of animals, for fear of unconsciously devouring some friend or kinsman.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phoenix is a birds (that renews and reproduces itself)
q: there is one bird which renews and reproduces itself. The Assyrians call it the Phœnix.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phoenix feeds on frankincense (in drops)
q: It lives not on corn or grass, but on drops of frankincense, and the juices of the amomum.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phoenix feeds on amomum (as juice)
q: It lives not on corn or grass, but on drops of frankincense, and the juices of the amomum.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phoenix builds nest (from cassia, spikenard, cinnamon and myrrh)
q: As soon as it has strewed in this cassia and ears of sweet spikenard and bruised cinnamon with yellow myrrh, it lays itself down on it, and finishes its life in the midst of odours.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Rome rises Dardanian Rome (according to report)
q: Now, too, there is a report that Dardanian Rome is rising; which, close to the waters of Tiber that rises in the Apennines, is laying the foundations of her greatness beneath a vast structure.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Rome is located near Tiber (whose waters rise in the Apennines)
q: Now, too, there is a report that Dardanian Rome is rising; which, close to the waters of Tiber that rises in the Apennines, is laying the foundations of her greatness beneath a vast structure.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Rome becomes mistress of the boundless earth (in the future)
q: She then, in her growth, is changing her form, and will one day be the mistress of the boundless earth.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras travels through Asia (according to the explanation)
q: Having travelled through Asia, it is supposed that Pythagoras passed into Italy, and settled at Crotona, to promulgate there the philosophical principles which he had acquired in his travels through Egypt and Asia Minor.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Troy is saved by Æneas (through the preservation of its descendant)
q: ‘Son of a Goddess, if thou dost thyself well understand the presentiment of my mind, Troy shall not, thou being preserved, entirely fall.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æneas carries Penates (from Troy)
q: Remembering it, I call to mind that Helenus prophesied this to Æneas, who bore the Penates {from Troy}

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Helenus prophesies Æneas (about Troy’s future and its settlement)
q: I call to mind that Helenus prophesied this to Æneas, who bore the Penates {from Troy}

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Octavius is adopted by Julius Cæsar
q: This was Octavius, the adopted son of Julius Cæsar.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Troy declines ruins (after formerly being great in wealth and men)
q: So Troy was great, both in her riches and her men, and for ten years could afford so much blood; {whereas}, now laid low, she only shows her ancient ruins, and, instead of her wealth, {she points at} the tombs of her ancestors.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nature changes everything (continually, while nothing perishes)
q: The principle of Pythagoras, that everything is continually changing and that nothing perishes, is true to a certain extent; but in his times, and even in those of Ovid, philosophy was not sufficiently advanced to speak with precision on the subject, and to discover the true boundary between truth and fiction.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: human beings should practice vegetarian abstinence (to avoid eating bodies that may contain related souls)
q: We too, {who are} a portion of the universe, (since we are not only bodies, but are fleeting souls as well, and can enter into beasts {as our} abode, and be hidden within the breasts of the cattle), should allow those bodies which may contain the souls of our parents, or of our brothers, or of those allied with us by some tie, or of men at all events, to be safe and unmolested; and we ought not to fill[51] our entrails with victuals fit for Thyestes.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras settles in Italy (at Crotona)
q: Having travelled through Asia, it is supposed that Pythagoras passed into Italy, and settled at Crotona, to promulgate there the philosophical principles which he had acquired in his travels through Egypt and Asia Minor.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras promulgates Pythagorean philosophy (at Crotona)
q: Having travelled through Asia, it is supposed that Pythagoras passed into Italy, and settled at Crotona, to promulgate there the philosophical principles which he had acquired in his travels through Egypt and Asia Minor.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is identified with Euphorbus (in a former incarnation)
q: indeed, the more strongly to enforce his doctrine by a personal illustration, he was in the habit of promulgating that he remembered to have been Euphorbus, at the time of the siege of Troy, and that his soul, after several other transmigrations, had at last entered the body which it then inhabited, under the name of Pythagoras.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagorean philosophy has feature metempsychosis (as one of its two main features)
q: Its main features may be reduced to two general heads; the first of which was the doctrine of the Metempsychosis, or continual transmigration of souls from one body into another.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagorean philosophy explains change and transformation (as changes in the physical world)
q: The second feature of this philosophy consisted in the elucidation of the changes that happen in the physical world, a long series of which is here set forth by the Poet; truth being mingled at random with fiction.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: metempsychosis is a doctrine of continual transmigration (of souls)
q: Its main features may be reduced to two general heads; the first of which was the doctrine of the Metempsychosis, or continual transmigration of souls from one body into another.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: metempsychosis transfers human souls (from one body into another)
q: Its main features may be reduced to two general heads; the first of which was the doctrine of the Metempsychosis, or continual transmigration of souls from one body into another.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius is a king (of the Roman people)
q: they say that Numa returned to his country, and, being voluntarily invited,[53] received the sovereignty of the Roman people.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nymph Egeria is transformed into fountain of Egeria (through grief and tears)
q: until, moved by her affection as she grieved, the sister of Phœbus formed a cool fountain from her body, and dissolved her limbs in ever-flowing waters.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: fountain of Egeria is a cool fountain (formed from Egeria's body)
q: the sister of Phœbus formed a cool fountain from her body, and dissolved her limbs in ever-flowing waters.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is a son of Theseus
q: the hero, the son of Theseus, say to her as she wept

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus has event death of Hippolytus (caused by frightened horses and a broken chariot)
q: The horses of Hippolytus being frightened by a sea-monster, he is killed by being thrown from his chariot

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: death of Hippolytus is caused by sea-monster (the monster frightens his horses)
q: The horses of Hippolytus being frightened by a sea-monster, he is killed by being thrown from his chariot

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus's chariot is broken by stump (at the wheel and long axle-tree)
q: had not the wheel, by running against a stump, been broken and disjoined just where it turns round on the long axle-tree.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus has event resurrection of Hippolytus (through the remedies of Apollo's son)
q: Nor could life have been restored me, but through the powerful remedies of the son of Apollo.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: resurrection of Hippolytus is opposed by Pluto (much against his will)
q: After I had received it, through potent herbs and the Pæonian aid,[56] much against the will of Pluto

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: resurrection of Hippolytus is enabled by Pæon (through potent herbs and medical aid)
q: After I had received it, through potent herbs and the Pæonian aid,[56] much against the will of Pluto

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is transformed into Virbius (by Diana, after his resurrection)
q: she said, ‘Thou, the same who wast Hippolytus, be thou now Virbius.’[57]

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius has wife Nymph Egeria (a Nymph)
q: Blest with a Nymph for his wife, and the Muses for his guides, he taught the rites of sacrifice, and brought over to the arts of peace a race inured to savage warfare.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Virbius is a lower God (hidden in Diana's grove)
q: From that time I have inhabited this grove; and, as one of the lower Gods, I lie concealed under the protection of my mistress

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Virbius is devoted to Diana (as his mistress and protector)
q: and to her am I devoted.”[58]

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Diana protects Virbius (in her grove)
q: as one of the lower Gods, I lie concealed under the protection of my mistress

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages is a diviner (the first teacher of Etruscan divination)
q: The natives called him Tages. He was the first to teach the Etrurian nation to foretell future events.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages arises from Tages's clod (in the midst of the fields)
q: the Etrurian ploughman beheld the fate-revealing clod in the midst of the fields move at first of its own accord and no one touching it, and afterwards assume a human form

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages teaches Etrurian nation (to foretell future events)
q: He was the first to teach the Etrurian nation to foretell future events.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages is associated with divination (through foretelling future events)
q: He was the first to teach the Etrurian nation to foretell future events.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus's lance is transformed into a tree with limber twigs (after being fixed in the Palatine hill)
q: Romulus once saw his lance, fixed in the Palatine hill, suddenly shoot forth; which {now} stood there with a root newly-formed, {and} not with the iron {point} driven in; and, now no longer as a dart, but as a tree with limber twigs

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus's lance provides shade (after its transformation into a tree)
q: it sent forth, for the admiring {spectators}, a shade that was not looked for.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nymph Egeria has husband Numa Pompilius
q: Blest with a Nymph for his wife, and the Muses for his guides, he taught the rites of sacrifice, and brought over to the arts of peace a race inured to savage warfare.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus has possession Cippus's horns (on his forehead)
q: Cippus beheld his horns in the water of the stream, (for he did see them)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus is offered kingship (by the Etrurian soothsayer's interpretation)
q: “Hail, O king! for thee, Cippus, thee and thy horns shall this place and the Latian towers obey.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus rejects kingship (rather than rule Rome)
q: Much more righteously shall I pass my life in exile, than if the Capitol were to see me a king.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus chooses exile (rather than being a king)
q: Much more righteously shall I pass my life in exile, than if the Capitol were to see me a king.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cippus's voluntary exile opposes him
q: He, indeed, was able to enter the open gates, but I have opposed him; although no one is more nearly allied with him than myself.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus is forbidden to enter the city
q: since thou art forbidden to enter the city, give thee as much land, as a mark of honour

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus receives land (as much as he can encircle with yoked oxen in one day)
q: give thee as much land, as a mark of honour, as thou canst, with the oxen yoked to the pressed plough, make the circuit of from the rising of the sun to its setting.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cippus's horns are represented on Rome (carved on the city's brass-adorned doorposts)
q: They carve, too, the horns, imitating their wondrous form, on the door-posts adorned with brass

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius is guided by Muses (in his teaching and rule)
q: Blest with a Nymph for his wife, and the Muses for his guides, he taught the rites of sacrifice, and brought over to the arts of peace a race inured to savage warfare.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orestes brings Diana (to Aricia)
q: the sacred rites of Diana, brought thither by Orestes

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Apollo has son the son of Apollo (whose remedies restore Hippolytus)
q: Nor could life have been restored me, but through the powerful remedies of the son of Apollo.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus has mother Hippolyta (according to one account)
q: Hippolytus was the son either of the Amazon Hippolyta, or Antiope.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus has mother Antiope (according to one account)
q: Hippolytus was the son either of the Amazon Hippolyta, or Antiope.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius teaches arts of peace (to a race inured to savage warfare)
q: he taught the rites of sacrifice, and brought over to the arts of peace a race inured to savage warfare.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius has event death of Numa (after finishing his reign and life, full of years)
q: After, full of years, he had finished his reign and his life, the Latian matrons and the people and the Senators lamented Numa at his death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: death of Numa is lamented by Romans
q: the Latian matrons and the people and the Senators lamented Numa at his death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: death of Numa is lamented by Latian matrons
q: the Latian matrons and the people and the Senators lamented Numa at his death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nymph Egeria is located in Aricia (in the thick groves of the valley)
q: But his wife, leaving the city, lay hid, concealed in the thick groves of the valley of Aricia

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid attributes study to Pythagoras (to Numa before his election to sovereignty)
q: Ovid, following the notion that was generally entertained of the wisdom of Numa, pretends that before he was elected to the sovereignty he went to Crotona, for the purpose of studying under Pythagoras;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Minos attributes ordinances to Jupiter (the first Minos; ordinances given to Crete)
q: The first Minos affirmed that Jupiter was the author of the ordinances which he gave to the people of Crete,

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Lycurgus attributes laws to Apollo (laws given to his people)
q: while Lycurgus attributed his to Apollo.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Dionysius of Halicarnassus describes Numa Pompilius (as ruling in peace and promoting piety, justice, and good laws)
q: The Romans affirm that Numa was never engaged in any warlike expedition; but that he passed his whole reign in profound peace: that his first care was to encourage piety and justice in his dominions, and to civilize his people by good and wholesome laws.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius rules in profound peace (throughout his reign, according to the Romans)
q: The Romans affirm that Numa was never engaged in any warlike expedition; but that he passed his whole reign in profound peace:

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius is considered inspired his profound skill in governing (by the Romans)
q: His profound skill in governing made him pass for being inspired, and gave rise to many fabulous stories.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius has secret interviews with Nymph Egeria (according to some accounts)
q: Some have said that he had secret interviews with the Nymph Egeria;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius consults Muses (according to some accounts)
q: others, that he frequently consulted one of the Muses, and was instructed by her in the art of government.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius seeks to confirm belief in communication with heaven (among the Roman people)
q: Numa was desirous to confirm the people in this opinion;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romans believe in conferences of Numa Pompilius with Nymph Egeria (so strongly that they searched for her)
q: The Romans were so persuaded of the fact of Numa’s conferences with the Nymph Egeria, that they went into the grove of Aricia to seek her;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid commits anachronism about Pythagoras (in connecting him with Numa)
q: but he is guilty of a considerable anachronism in this instance, as Pythagoras was not born till very many years after the time of Numa.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nymph Egeria is associated with fountain (the Romans found it in her grove)
q: but finding nothing but a fountain in the spot which he used to frequent, they promulgated the story of the transformation of the Nymph.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius uses Hydromancy (for divination with the fountain’s waters)
q: St. Augustin, speaking on this subject, says that Numa made use of the waters of that fountain in the divination which was performed by the aid of water, and was called Hydromancy.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hydromancy is a divination (performed by the aid of water)
q: the divination which was performed by the aid of water, and was called Hydromancy.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Theseus leaves Ariadne (in Naxos)
q: Theseus having left Ariadne in the isle of Naxos, flattered himself with the hopes of marrying her sister Phædra.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ariadne is left in Naxos (by Theseus)
q: Theseus having left Ariadne in the isle of Naxos, flattered himself with the hopes of marrying her sister Phædra.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Deucalion succeeds Minos (as ruler of Crete immediately after Minos’s death)
q: Deucalion, succeeding Minos in Crete immediately after his death, sent Phædra to Athens.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phædra is sent to Athens (by Deucalion)
q: Deucalion, succeeding Minos in Crete immediately after his death, sent Phædra to Athens.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phædra falls in love with Hippolytus (after arriving in Athens)
q: On arriving there, she fell in love with Hippolytus, the son of Theseus, who had been brought up at Trœzen by Pittheus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is a son of Theseus
q: she fell in love with Hippolytus, the son of Theseus, who had been brought up at Trœzen by Pittheus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is brought up at Trœzen (by Pittheus)
q: Hippolytus, the son of Theseus, who had been brought up at Trœzen by Pittheus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius precedes Servius Tullius (the sixth Roman king)
q: According to Livy, Pythagoras flourished in the time of Servius Tullius, the sixth Roman king, about one hundred and fifty years after Numa.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phædra builds Hippolyteum (near Trœzen, to see Hippolytus more often)
q: she built a temple to Venus near Trœzen, that she might the more frequently have the opportunity of seeing Hippolytus, and called it by the name of Hippolyteum.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is described as wise and chaste (according to Euripides; hostile to voluptuousness)
q: According to Euripides, this youth was wise, chaste, and an enemy to all voluptuousness.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus pursues hunting and chariot racing (as exercises of a high-status youth)
q: He spent his time in hunting and chariot racing, with other exercises which formed the pursuits of youths of high station.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phædra accuses Hippolytus (in a letter to Theseus)
q: having first written a letter to inform him that she could not survive an attempt which Hippolytus had made on her virtue.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Theseus invokes Neptune (against Hippolytus)
q: On this, Theseus implored the assistance of Neptune, who sent a monster out of the sea, to frighten his horses, as he was driving along the sea-shore:

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Neptune sends sea monster (to frighten Theseus’s horses)
q: Theseus implored the assistance of Neptune, who sent a monster out of the sea, to frighten his horses, as he was driving along the sea-shore:

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus dies in chariot accident (after his horses were frightened by Neptune’s monster)
q: on which, they took fright, and throwing him from his chariot, he was killed.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: people of Trœzen honor Hippolytus (with divine honors after his death)
q: The people of Trœzen, regretting his loss, decreed him divine honours, built a temple, and appointed a priest to offer yearly sacrifices to him.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras flourishes in time of Servius Tullius (according to Livy)
q: According to Livy, Pythagoras flourished in the time of Servius Tullius, the sixth Roman king, about one hundred and fifty years after Numa.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: young women of Trœzen dedicate hair to Hippolytus (before marriage)
q: Euripides says, that the young women of Trœzen, when about to be married, cut off their hair and carried it to the temple of Hippolytus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is translated to heavens (according to the promulgated story)
q: It was also promulgated that the Gods had translated him to the heavens, where he was changed into the Constellation, called by the Latins ‘Auriga,’ or ‘the Charioteer.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is changed into Auriga (the constellation called the Charioteer)
q: where he was changed into the Constellation, called by the Latins ‘Auriga,’ or ‘the Charioteer.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius restores to life Hippolytus (according to later authors)
q: Later authors, whom Ovid here follows, added, that Æsculapius restored him to life, and that he afterwards appeared in Italy under the name of Virbius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus is known as Virbius (after appearing in Italy)
q: he afterwards appeared in Italy under the name of Virbius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: ancient Etrurians practice divination (especially by entrail inspection and bird-flight observation)
q: The ancient Etrurians were great adepts in the art of divination; their favourite method of exercising which was by the inspection of the entrails of beasts, and the observation of the flight of birds;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: divination spreads from ancient Etrurians (over the whole of Italy)
q: and from them, as we learn from Cicero in his book on Divination, the system spread over the whole of Italy.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages is considered first teacher of divination (in Etruria)
q: Tages is supposed to have been the first who taught this art, and he wrote treatises upon it, which, according to Plutarch, were quoted by ancient authors.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Crotona is built during reign of Numa Pompilius (in the fourth year)
q: Besides, Dionysius of Halicarnassus distinctly asserts that the city of Crotona was only built in the fourth year of the reign of Numa Pompilius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages is called son of the earth (because his origin and parentage were unknown)
q: It not being known whence he came, or who were his parents, he was called, in the language of the poets, a son of the earth.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus throws spear of Romulus (from Mount Aventine toward the Capitol)
q: Ovid next makes a passing allusion to the spear of Romulus, which, when thrown by him from the Mount Aventine towards the Capitol, sticking in the ground was converted into a tree, which immediately put forth leaves.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: spear of Romulus is converted into Romulus's lance (after sticking in the ground)
q: when thrown by him from the Mount Aventine towards the Capitol, sticking in the ground was converted into a tree, which immediately put forth leaves.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus's lance is a presage of future greatness of Rome (according to Roman interpretation)
q: This prodigy was taken for a presage of the future greatness of Rome:

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Republic flourishes while Romulus's lance (according to Plutarch’s account)
q: Plutarch, in his life of Romulus, says that so long as this tree stood, the Republic flourished.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus is a Roman figure associated with a prodigy (in Roman historical tradition)
q: The story of Genucius Cippus is one of those strange fables with which the Roman history is diversified.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus develops horn-like growths (on his forehead, according to the story)
q: He says that Cippus, going one day out of Rome, suddenly found that something which resembled horns was growing out of his forehead.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: augurs predict for Genucius Cippus (kingship if he re-entered Rome)
q: he consulted the augurs, who said that he would be chosen king, if he ever entered the city again.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus chooses voluntary banishment (to avoid becoming king and preserve Rome from monarchy)
q: As the royal power was abhorred in Rome, he preferred a voluntary banishment to revisiting Rome on those terms.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romans erect brazen statue (of Genucius Cippus with horns over the gate of departure)
q: Struck with this heroism, the Romans erected a brazen statue with horns over the gate by which he departed,

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius retires to Arician grove (habitually, to consult Nymph Egeria)
q: Numa is said to have been in the habit of retiring to the Arician grove, to consult the Nymph Egeria upon the laws which he was about to promulgate for the benefit of his subjects.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus receives lands (from the Senate, as a reward for patriotism)
q: The Senate also conferred certain lands on Cippus, as a reward for his patriotism.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus returns to Rome (in Ovid’s version, after assisting Consul Valerius)
q: The fact is, however, as Ovid represents it, that Cippus was not going out of Rome, but returning to it, when the prodigy happened; he having been to convey assistance to the Consul Valerius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius consults Nymph Egeria (about laws for his subjects)
q: Numa is said to have been in the habit of retiring to the Arician grove, to consult the Nymph Egeria upon the laws which he was about to promulgate for the benefit of his subjects.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Nymph Egeria is a nymph
q: Numa is said to have been in the habit of retiring to the Arician grove, to consult the Nymph Egeria upon the laws which he was about to promulgate for the benefit of his subjects.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Apollo is a God (Phœbus)
q: thou hast no need of Apollo to diminish thy grief, but of the son of Apollo.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius is a son of Apollo
q: thou hast no need of Apollo to diminish thy grief, but of the son of Apollo.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius is a son of Coronis
q: the Island surrounded by the channel of the Tiber introduced the son of Coronis into the sacred rites of the City of Romulus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius is a God (saving and health-restoring)
q: the saving God seemed, O Roman, to be standing before thy couch

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius is a restorer of health (to Rome)
q: And {thus} did he come, the restorer of health, to the City.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Epidaurians possess Æsculapius (as their protector and guardian Deity)
q: Many refused it, and advised them not to part with their own protector, and to give up their own guardian Deity.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: ambassadors are sent to Epidaurus
q: they sent some to reach the coasts of Epidaurus[62] with the winds

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Rome is a City of Romulus
q: whence {it is that} the Island surrounded by the channel of the Tiber introduced the son of Coronis into the sacred rites of the City of Romulus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: serpent is a form of Æsculapius (divine transformation)
q: Into this shall I be changed; but I shall be greater, and I shall appear to be of a size as great as that into which heavenly bodies ought to be transformed.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: serpent is a God (recognized by the Epidaurian priest)
q: The God! Behold the God! Whoever you are that are present, be of good omen, both with your words and your feelings.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: serpent has attribute golden (in the temple at Epidaurus)
q: the God, all glittering with gold, in {the form of} a serpent, with crest erect

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ausonian ship transports serpent (from Epidaurus toward Rome)
q: he places his body in the Ausonian ship.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tiber surrounds Island of the Tiber (by its channel)
q: the Island surrounded by the channel of the Tiber

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Island of the Tiber is surrounded by the river (where the river is divided into two parts)
q: There is a spot, where} the river flowing around, is divided into two parts; it is called “the Island.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Island of the Tiber introduces Æsculapius cult (into Rome)
q: whence {it is that} the Island surrounded by the channel of the Tiber introduced the son of Coronis into the sacred rites of the City of Romulus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius cult is introduced into Rome (after the serpent's arrival)
q: From this period, which was about the year of Rome 462, the worship of Æsculapius was introduced in the city

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius cult is used for disease (especially during pestilence)
q: to him recourse was had in cases of disease, and especially in times of pestilence.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Rome has air Latian air
q: A dire contagion had once infected the Latian air

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tiber Island temple is built on Island of the Tiber (for Æsculapius)
q: as they, in their credulity, fancied that the God had chosen the place for his habitation, they built a temple there in his honour.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Temple of Æsculapius is built for Æsculapius (on the Island of the Tiber)
q: they built a temple there in his honour.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romans are descendants of Æneas
q: the descendants of Æneas rejoice

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Vesta has attendants Romans (those who tend her fires)
q: Hither, all the people indiscriminately, a crowd both of matrons and of men, rush to meet him; they, too, Vesta! who tend thy fires

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Roman Sibylline books are consulted for pestilence (to determine how it might cease)
q: The resources of physic having been exhausted, the Sibylline books were consulted to ascertain by what expedient the calamity might be put an end to

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Roman Sibylline books direct bringing Æsculapius (from Epidaurus to Rome)
q: they found that the plague would not cease till they had brought Æsculapius from Epidaurus to Rome.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: pestilence ravages Rome (frightfully)
q: Under the consulate of Quintus Fabius Gurges, and Decimus Junius Brutus Scæva, Rome was ravaged by a frightful pestilence.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: pestilence is a contagion
q: A dire contagion had once infected the Latian air

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: disease dries up blood (through consumption)
q: the pale bodies were deformed by a consumption that dried up the blood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Delphi is a oracle of Phœbus
q: they repaired to Delphi which occupies the centre spot of the world, the oracle of Phœbus

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Delphi occupies centre spot of the world
q: they repaired to Delphi which occupies the centre spot of the world

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Julius Cæsar is a Deity (in Rome)
q: Cæsar is a Deity in his own city

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus is deified during lifetime Deity (according to the explanation)
q: Augustus, however, had not to wait for death to receive divine honours, as he enjoyed the glory of seeing himself worshipped as a Deity and adored at altars erected to him, even in his lifetime.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus has a reign Augustus’s reign (long and glorious)
q: while he promises him a long and glorious reign.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus intercedes for Julius Cæsar (seeking his apotheosis)
q: by the intercession of Venus, his ancestor, he is changed into a star.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus rescues Julius Cæsar (by carrying his soul to heaven)
q: the genial Venus, perceived by none, stood in the very midst of the Senate-house, and snatched the soul, just liberated {from the body}, away from the limbs of her own Cæsar

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid is a Poet
q: whatever other {Deities} it is lawful and righteous for a Poet to invoke

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid completes The Metamorphoses (at the end of his work)
q: And now I have completed a work

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid expects Ovid’s immortality through poetry (through lasting fame)
q: Yet, in my better part, I shall be raised immortal above the lofty stars, and indelible shall be my name.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ovid’s immortality through poetry is read by the lips of nations (throughout all ages)
q: And wherever the Roman power is extended throughout the vanquished earth, I shall be read by the lips of nations, and (if the presages of Poets have aught of truth) throughout all ages shall I survive in fame.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Julius Cæsar is the father of Augustus
q: For of {all} the acts of Cæsar, there is not one more ennobling than that he was the father of this {our Cæsar}.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Metamorphoses is a completed work (covering history from the beginning of the world to Ovid’s time)
q: The Poet having fulfilled his promise, and having brought down his work from the beginning of the world to his own times

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Gods are unable to prevent assassination of Julius Cæsar (because of Fate)
q: Although they were not able to frustrate the iron decrees of the aged sisters

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: conspirators plot against Julius Cæsar (with treachery)
q: Behold, on how vast a scale treason is plotted against me, and with how great perfidy that life is sought

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Julius Cæsar’s apotheosis is a deification (represented as transformation into a star)
q: by the intercession of Venus, his ancestor, he is changed into a star.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Julius Cæsar is transformed into star of Julius Cæsar (after death)
q: And as she bore it, she perceived it assume a {train of} light and become inflamed; and she dropped it from her bosom. Above the moon it takes its flight, and, as a star, it glitters, carrying a flaming train with a lengthened track

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: assassination of Julius Cæsar occurs in Senate-house (through conspiratorial treachery)
q: no other place in the {whole} City than the Senate-house pleased them for this crime and this atrocious murder.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus’s reign includes Roman law and civil rights (after peace is granted to the earth)
q: Peace being granted to the earth, he will turn his attention to civil rights, and, as a most upright legislator, he will enact laws.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Julius Cæsar is assassinated in Senate-house
q: drawn swords were carried into a temple; and no other place in the {whole} City than the Senate-house pleased them for this crime and this atrocious murder.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus is a ruler (of the earth)
q: Jupiter rules the abodes of heaven and the realms of the threefold world:[92] the earth is under Augustus

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus is the son of Julius Cæsar (as his heir in glory)
q: Thou, with his son, who, as the heir to his glory, will bear the burden of government devolving {on him}

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus enacts Roman law and civil rights (as an upright legislator)
q: Peace being granted to the earth, he will turn his attention to civil rights, and, as a most upright legislator, he will enact laws.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Augustus regulates manners (after his own example)
q: After his own example, too, will he regulate manners

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager is a son of Œneus
q: But the hand of the son of Œneus has different success

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager leads Calydonian boar chase
q: His son Meleager leads the chase

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager loves Atalanta (against the will of the God)
q: the Calydonian hero both beheld, and at the same moment sighed for her, against the will of the God

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager kills Plexippus (after Plexippus takes Atalanta's prize)
q: with his cruel sword, he pierced the breast of Plexippus

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager kills Toxeus (after Toxeus's brother is killed)
q: Nor suffered he Toxeus, who was doubtful what to do, and both wishful to avenge his brother, and fearing his brother’s fate, long to be in doubt; but a second time warmed his weapon, reeking with the former slaughter, in the blood of the brother.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Meleager dies by fatal billet (when it is consumed by fire)
q: Unsuspecting, and at a distance, Meleager is burned by that flame, and feels his entrails scorched by the secret fires

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is a daughter of the king of Arcadia
q: Atalanta, the daughter of the king of Arcadia

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
